video_title: Why AI Compute Comes in Rectangles — Erik Bernhardsson, Modal
gist: Modal CEO Erik Bernhardsson explains how GPU scarcity has pushed the market into rigid three-year prepaid 'rectangles' of capacity, and why Modal positions itself as a duration-transformation aggregator that pools ~25 clouds and thousands of customers' bursty demand into on-demand compute. He details neocloud financial engineering, the risk of a GPU price collapse, a possible 2027 shift to non-Nvidia accelerators, and Modal's growth (~50x in two years, sandboxes at one-third of revenue growing ~30% a month).

insights.claim: Modal now sources GPUs from almost 25 clouds and, to get the capacity it needs, increasingly must sign three-plus-year deals with meaningful upfront prepayment and locked-in pricing; until end of last year most capacity was hyperscaler spot or one-year reservations.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Signals a structural shift from spot/short-term to long-dated, prepaid GPU contracts, favoring capacity owners and neoclouds.
insights.quote: We actually work with almost 25 clouds at this point

insights.claim: Modal has built a four-person full-time procurement desk calling neoclouds and a ~10-person engineering team just to manage rented bare-metal capacity (network issues, bad drives, GPUs falling off the bus).
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: GPU procurement is becoming an operational/financial function even for software-first infra companies, raising barriers to entry.

insights.claim: Bernhardsson rejects the idea that GPUs are a cornered resource: Nvidia is shipping several hundred thousand Blackwells a month and anyone willing to pay a high price can get capacity; he likens 'must buy now' panic to the pandemic toilet-paper shortage.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Argues against scarcity-forever narratives that underpin neocloud and GPU-lessor valuations.
insights.quote: Nvidia is delivering, you know, several hundred thousand black walls, you know, a month

insights.claim: Hardware prices normally fall 'like gravity'; the current period of rising GPU prices could last anywhere from another 6 to 36 months, and the bigger risk he sees is a price collapse that would hurt anyone who locked in a lot of supply at the top.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Players with heavy long-dated GPU commitments (neoclouds, resellers) carry tail risk of buying at the peak.
insights.quote: I do worry more about actually prices collapsing

insights.claim: Because Modal holds many reservations at fixed rates and can pass scarcity pricing to customers, it is effectively long GPU prices, so rising prices are not necessarily bad for it.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Fixed-rate reservation books act as an embedded long position on compute prices for aggregators.

insights.claim: Today's GPU scarcity rent is captured primarily by Nvidia and secondarily by neoclouds/anyone owning capacity, but he doubts owning GPUs earns enough long-run premium to justify holding the balance-sheet risk.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Frames where the profit pool in AI compute sits now versus later; cautious on long-term asset-owner economics.
insights.quote: there's a scarcity rent, right? Like who captured the scarcity rent? I think that primarily goes to two places mostly Nvidia

insights.claim: Over-buying GPUs to resell is risky because downside events are correlated: prices fall, utilization falls and the resale market vanishes at the same time; he cites the Hunt brothers' failed silver corner as a warning against cornering the market.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Liquidity of GPU secondary markets cannot be relied on in a downturn—relevant for GPU-backed lending and lessors.
insights.quote: prices going down and utilization going down and the market for reselling capacity goes vanishes at the kind of the same time

insights.claim: Nvidia appears to prefer diversified buyers and gives neoclouds/alternative clouds more allocation, while Anthropic and OpenAI prefer large blocks from tried-and-true vendors for training, leaving smaller, riskier clusters (e.g., 32 nodes in Armenia, 128 in Indonesia) as an opportunity for aggregators like Modal.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Fragmented long-tail GPU supply is a niche that aggregators can harvest at good prices.
insights.quote: you can get 32 nodes in Armenia, you can get 128 nodes in Indonesia

insights.claim: Modal vets GPU vendors with a spec sheet (IOPS, CPU benchmark scores, north-south bandwidth, egress/ingress) and single-node acceptance tests, but still sometimes signs tens to hundreds of millions of dollars of commitments with vendors it doesn't fully know, keeping an internal reliability/responsiveness ranking akin to SemiAnalysis's ClusterMAX.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Shows counterparty risk and the importance of vendor reliability scoring in the neocloud ecosystem.

insights.claim: Modal currently rents all capacity and prefers to remain a lean software company not owning hard assets, but says everything is on the table for 2027 capacity—including buying, joint ventures or SPV-style structures—while noting equity-funded hardware is very dilutive and debt requires locked-in long-term revenue.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Watch for Modal (and similar PLG infra players) moving toward asset ownership or structured financing.

insights.claim: AI investment is approaching several percentage points of US GDP and he notes US interest rates shooting up in recent weeks, describing neoclouds as very sophisticated financial-engineering companies.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Macro link between AI capex financing and rates; neoclouds are levered financial plays as much as tech.

themes.theme: Neocloud financing & compute as an asset class

insights.claim: Neoclouds scale extremely fast by pre-selling capacity: they sign multi-year chip contracts with a big buyer like Anthropic or OpenAI, take that contract to Wall Street to raise money, then buy hardware from Supermicro/Dell/Nvidia and deliver it; he cites Nscale going from nowhere to hundreds of billions in pipeline despite barely having capacity.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Neocloud growth is contract-backed financial engineering; their risk is concentrated in counterparty and refinancing.
insights.quote: you can basically sort of pre-ell things that you haven't even bought

insights.claim: A PLG company like Modal cannot lock in long-term contracts the same way, so it is financially harder for it to scale capacity as fast as neoclouds, though he expects to get there long-term.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Capital intensity is a structural disadvantage for usage-based infra vs. contract-backed neoclouds.

insights.claim: Startups such as Silicon Data and Compute Exchange are building GPU price indices and derivatives; he welcomes better hedging/insurance but doubts GPUs become a Henry Hub/Brent-style commoditized asset because compute is heterogeneous (network, location, disks, CPUs, reliability).
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Tempers expectations for liquid GPU futures markets, though risk-sharing tools are needed at current scale.

insights.claim: Posting a tweet about an IPO-ready startup in a capex arms race wanting to 'pace the arms race', Bernhardsson declined to comment.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Hints at insider perception that frontier-lab capex competition is partly a coordination problem; low signal.

themes.theme: Rectangles vs. on-demand: Modal's aggregation model

insights.claim: The biggest downside of GPU scarcity is that almost all capacity is sold as a three-year 'rectangle' starting 3-6 months in the future, which doesn't match real demand that varies daily, grows and bursts.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Creates a market for a 'duration transformation' layer that resells flexible capacity—Modal's core pitch.
insights.quote: almost all capacity is sold as three years as a three-year rectangle starting 3 to 6 months in the future

insights.claim: Modal's value prop reduces to two things—developer experience and capacity—and it acts as a duration transformer, aggregating many thousands of customers whose bursty demand smooths in aggregate so it can buy rectangles and sell on-demand slices (e.g., 100 GPUs immediately without talking to sales).
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: An aggregator earns a spread between rigid long-term supply and flexible demand, akin to bank maturity transformation.
insights.quote: we're aggregating the world's compute capacity and we're very good at slicing it out like very granularly

insights.claim: Inference providers should structurally exist separately from model builders because the best open model keeps changing (e.g., each new Chinese lab release shifts demand), and a pooled provider can reallocate GPUs between models seamlessly, whereas labs holding their own capacity face boom-bust utilization.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Supports the independent inference-provider business model against vertical integration by labs.
insights.quote: There's an interesting structural reason why in inference providers should exist separately from model builders

insights.claim: Modal deliberately avoided becoming a neocloud selling rectangular multi-year GPU blocks, treating its capacity as one global pool across regions rather than per-region clusters—an early 'fateful' decision.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Differentiates Modal's model from CoreWeave-style neoclouds; global pooling underpins utilization.

insights.claim: Cash for capacity prepayments is Modal's best use of capital; salaries and offices are a rounding error versus GPU spend, giving the business 'insane' operating leverage with ~200 employees.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Infra-aggregator economics are dominated by compute COGS and prepayment financing, not opex.
insights.quote: in the grand scheme of like our our uh financials like it's it's basically a rounding error right now

insights.claim: Modal's top focus is capacity and its financial complexity—pricing/packaging and the own-vs-rent tension, including whether to move in a more neocloud direction or the opposite.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Signals strategic optionality: Modal could become more capital-intensive.

insights.claim: Modal has grown at least ~50x in revenue, users and usage over roughly two years.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Indicates hypergrowth in AI infra demand for serverless GPU platforms.
insights.quote: it's probably like at least like 50x in terms of like revenue and users and usage

insights.claim: Modal's revenue went from ~$100/month in November 2022 to ~$2,000 the next month and ~$30,000 in January 2023, driven by Stable Diffusion inference; one customer (likely Mage) was 80-90% of Q1 2023 revenue, then Suno became a big chunk in late 2023, and revenue is now well diversified.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Shows how generative-AI killer apps drive infra adoption and early customer concentration risk.

insights.claim: Modal Functions (serverless, mostly inference) is about two-thirds of revenue and Modal Sandboxes about one-third; customers include Decagon, Suno, Runway, Cognition, Lovable and Ramp.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Revenue mix shows agent/code-execution compute becoming a major infra category alongside inference.

insights.claim: Modal recently crossed 200 employees (~150 engineers), grew headcount ~4x in 12 months, expects ~250 by year-end and possibly ~700 next year at 2.5-3x growth, mostly systems engineers plus sales; it is also building a research team for post-training, distillation and quantization.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Aggressive hiring plans signal strong revenue expectations and expansion into new products.

insights.claim: Modal scaled forward-deployed engineers from about 4 to about 24 this year to do LLM performance tuning (training draft models, tweaking vLLM/SGLang), migrations and catching overprovisioning, with the explicit goal of turning FDE work into self-serve product rather than becoming services-heavy.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: FDE-led go-to-market is spreading in AI infra; watch for services margin dilution vs. productization.

insights.claim: Modal remains a 'cloud maximalist' with no plans for on-prem, viewing on-prem/BYOC/VPC peering as legacy security models; it quotes very high prices for BYOC (no one has accepted), though BYOC could be a way to run Modal on neolabs' existing reservations and pool that capacity.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Multi-tenant cloud is seen as winning; BYOC could become a capacity-sourcing channel rather than a security feature.
insights.quote: to me onrem looks increasingly like sort of a legacy business model

insights.claim: Modal Sandboxes launched in 2023 with almost no traction for two years—the team considered shutting it down—then exploded as LLMs got good at generating full apps, driven by vibe-coding firms like Lovable, background agents at Ramp and neolabs doing reinforcement learning on sandboxes.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Agent code execution and RL environments are a fast-growing compute demand category.

insights.claim: Sandbox revenue keeps growing about 30% every month even as Bernhardsson repeatedly expects it to plateau.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Implies ~20x annualized growth in agent sandbox compute—a strong demand signal for the category.
insights.quote: Every month I keep saying our sandbox revenue might have plateaued but it keeps going up 30% every month

insights.claim: Bernhardsson believes Modal has by far the largest market share in sandboxes because it can run hundreds of thousands to millions of them reliably, while acknowledging the sandbox space itself is not very differentiated.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Scale and reliability, not features, may decide winners in a commoditizing sandbox market.

insights.claim: He predicts sandboxes will shift from 'dev box in the cloud' lift-and-shift to ephemeral environments—potentially one per command with snapshotting to pause/resume/fork—with agents decoupled from sandboxes as long-running durable-execution workflows; Modal's median sandbox already lasts about 8 seconds.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Favors providers with fast snapshotting/startup; suggests usage-based compute volume per agent will explode.
insights.quote: I think the median soundbox in modal today is like 8 seconds long

insights.claim: Cutting sandbox start/stop overhead could transform CI: snapshot after setup, then clone to run every test in its own sandbox (a thousand in parallel), which today is blocked by per-shard setup overhead (Amdahl's law).
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Potential disruption vector for CI vendors from ephemeral-sandbox infrastructure.

insights.claim: Anthropic's managed agents offer a bring-your-own-sandbox integration that supports Modal; Bernhardsson reads this as Anthropic rationally maximizing ecosystem surface area since it monetizes inference.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Frontier labs partnering rather than vertically integrating sandboxes leaves room for independent agent infra.

insights.claim: In the Hugging Face incident, agents exploited a vulnerable customer app deployed on Modal as a springboard to full internet access; Modal itself wasn't hacked, but it is exploring more restrictive security defaults (like AWS made public S3 buckets harder) and now uses agents internally to try to escape its sandboxes.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Agent-driven exploits raise security-default expectations for compute platforms.

insights.claim: After years of wrongly predicting it, Bernhardsson thinks 2027 might finally be the year of non-Nvidia accelerators, citing improving AMD scores, Google's TPUs, Trainium's software work, and Cerebras/Groq; he sees software as the main fix needed.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Potential erosion of Nvidia's share in inference beginning 2027.
insights.quote: I do think 2027 might be the year of non- Nvidia accelerators finally

insights.claim: TSMC and ASML may be a deeper bottleneck than Nvidia, and he expects Nvidia's monopoly not to last indefinitely.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Supply-chain chokepoints may matter more than accelerator vendor choice.

insights.claim: Disaggregated inference is emerging, e.g., running prefill on Nvidia and decode on Cerebras, mixing compute-bound and memory-bound hardware.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Heterogeneous inference stacks could create demand for alternative chips and orchestration software.

insights.claim: Open-source models (e.g., Kimi K3, DeepSeek 4.1, GLM 5.3) are now nearly as good as frontier models at much lower cost, making fine-tuning optional rather than necessary to reach frontier quality, though post-training/RL demand persists.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Open models compress frontier pricing power and shift the value of fine-tuning platforms.
insights.quote: they're like basically almost as good as like the Frontier model at a much lower cost

insights.claim: Bernhardsson does not view frontier LLMs as pure commodities: like Taylor Swift albums, labs can be good businesses as long as they repeatedly release new models with margins that amortize training costs.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Frontier-lab economics depend on release cadence and per-model margin, not permanent moats.

insights.claim: He is bullish on small/mid-size training (researchers, speech models, computational biology on ~64 GPUs, recommendation systems), batch jobs (one customer transcribed 5,000 years of audio in days) and low-latency voice as underserved infra markets.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Mid-market training and batch are under-served segments outside hyperscaler mega-deals.

insights.claim: Verifiable domains like coding, math and cybersecurity improve fastest via RL; next likely beneficiaries are computational biology/drug discovery and materials science where simulation or synthesis creates feedback loops, while diffuse-target domains will stay human-competitive longer.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Points to drug and materials discovery as next AI application waves.

insights.claim: Because of agent training data, it has become hard for Modal to deprecate APIs—agents favor old syntax—so Modal is more conservative on removals and runs internal benchmarks asking agents to deploy Stable Diffusion or rank sandbox vendors to track whether Modal is recommended.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Agent-engine optimization is a new distribution channel; incumbent presence in training data is a moat.
insights.quote: because of agent training data it's very hard to deprecate things now

insights.claim: He believes agent-driven discovery (like SEO) is won primarily through content, notes agents often misunderstand pricing, and concedes auto-generated 'slop' content would probably work though he dislikes the idea.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Developer-tool marketing is shifting to optimizing for LLM recommendations.

insights.claim: He argues incumbent cybersecurity companies are not 'cooked' because they sell fear/brand, enterprise relationships and blame-transfer, though AI agents may cut startups' human pentest cadence (e.g., from every six months to yearly).
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Pushback on the AI-kills-security-vendors narrative; services like pentesting more exposed than platforms.

insights.claim: Modal treats code reviews as optional, relying instead on heavy CI/CD investment, rate limits, decoupled systems and agent-written tests, and sees AI accelerating a cultural swing from management back to individual contributors.
insights.speaker: Erik Bernhardsson
insights.so_what: Illustrates AI-era engineering org changes that raise per-engineer leverage.
